title: Delete the group column. Then what?
hook: A lender trains a model without the group column. How will its approvals compare?

knows: a model can inherit bias from its data (whose-cutoff-wins)
doesNotKnow: that deleting the protected column does not stop a model learning from biased past decisions, because a correlated feature (here neighbourhood) carries the group, and the gap can grow

misconception: If the group column is removed from the data, the model cannot treat the groups differently.
objective: The learner can explain that a model trained on biased past approvals, seeing only neighbourhood, approved 80% of A and 20% of B because neighbourhood stood in for group, and that with mixed neighbourhoods the gap vanished.

claims.text: In the toy, 50 applicants are in group A and 50 in group B, and past lenders approved 80% of group A and 40% of group B in both neighbourhoods (stage header: 'Past lenders approved ○ A 80%, ▢ B 40%'). The toy model approves a whole neighbourhood if more than half of its past applicants there were approved (question: 'approves a whole one if most past applicants there were approved').
claims.source: The toy's own data and rule, world() in Demo.tsx (MODEL block), stated on the stage and in the explore hint. Dot positions inside each box are shuffled with mulberry32 seed 1 (first seed, untuned; positions change no number). | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. world() in Demo.tsx: PER_GROUP 50 per group; PAST A 0.8, B 0.4, the same in every neighbourhood; approve = past > 0.5. Stage header 'Past lenders approved ○ A 80%, ▢ B 40%' and explore hint ('approves a whole neighbourhood if most past applicants there were approved') match. layout() uses mulberry32(1) only to shuffle dot order.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14): the model's rule moved from the explore hint into the question (learner r10); previously verified by fact-checker on 2026-10-14. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Re-check after the W-839 wording change. Demo.tsx world(): PER_GROUP 50 per group; PAST A 0.8, B 0.4 in every neighbourhood; approve = past > 0.5. Stage header 'Past lenders approved ○ A 80%, ▢ B 40%' and the question's new rule text ('approves a whole one if most past applicants there were approved') both match the code; 'most' = more than half = past > 0.5.

claims.text: With 80% of each group in its own neighbourhood (40 A + 10 B in N1, 10 A + 40 B in N2), N1's past approval rate is 72% and N2's 48%, so the toy model approves N1 and rejects N2: A 80%, B 20%, a wider gap than the lenders' 80% and 40%. With 90% together: N1 76%, N2 44%; A 90%, B 10%.
claims.source: Arithmetic: (32 + 4)/50 = 72%, (8 + 16)/50 = 48%; (36 + 2)/50 = 76%, (4 + 18)/50 = 44%. world() in Demo.tsx; cm-ai brief check (node, 2026-10-14). Reveal values recorded when the learner presses 'Train without group'. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own arithmetic in node: seg 0.8 -> N1 40 A + 10 B, past (32 + 4)/50 = 72% approve; N2 10 A + 40 B, (8 + 16)/50 = 48% reject; A 40/50 = 80%, B 10/50 = 20% (gap 60 points, wider than 40). seg 0.9 -> N1 76%, N2 44%; A 90%, B 10%. The reveal quotes rec.q, recorded on 'Train without group' (seg 0.8).

claims.text: With mixed neighbourhoods (25 A + 25 B in each), both past rates are 60%, so neighbourhood no longer tracks group and the model approves everyone ('When you mixed the neighbourhoods, neighbourhood no longer tracked group, so the model could not tell them apart: it approved everyone'; stage: A 100% · B 100%).
claims.source: (20 + 10)/50 = 60% > 50% in both neighbourhoods. world(0.5) in Demo.tsx. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. seg 0.5 -> 25 A + 25 B in each; past (20 + 10)/50 = 60% > 50% in both, so both approved: A 100%, B 100%. 'mixed-seen' is a required milestone, so the reveal's 'When you mixed the neighbourhoods' always follows a seen run.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14): reveal wording for the mixed case changed (learner r10); previously verified by fact-checker on 2026-10-14. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Re-check after the W-839 reveal change. seg 0.5 -> mk(25, 25) in each neighbourhood: past (25 x 0.8 + 25 x 0.4)/50 = 60% > 50%, so both approved, A 100%, B 100%. The reveal sentence 'When you mixed the neighbourhoods ... it approved everyone' always follows a seen mixed run ('mixed-seen' is in MILESTONES and minInteractions = MILESTONES.length).

claims.text: Removing a protected attribute does not prevent discrimination when other features, such as where people live, are correlated with it ('Deleting the column deletes the label, not the pattern. Fairness has to be checked on outcomes by group, not on inputs').
claims.source: Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan, Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities (MIT Press, 2023; fairmlbook.org), chapter 3 ('Classification'), on why removing the sensitive attribute fails (redundant encodings); Pedreshi, Ruggieri and Turini (2008), 'Discrimination-aware data mining', KDD 2008 (redlining). About real systems. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD. No source that supports it could be opened from this host: the cited hosts return proxy 403 or fail DNS, and only GitHub raw, PyPI and npm are reachable. I did not verify it from memory or from search snippets. Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan (fairmlbook.org) and Pedreshi et al. 2008 could not be opened, and no GitHub source copy of the book was found. The toy shows the mechanism, but the claim is about real systems.
claims.note: FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Learner text (Demo.tsx lines 104-105): 'Deleting the column deletes the label, not the pattern. Fairness has to be checked on outcomes by group, not on inputs.' Opened on PMC: Adams-Prassl, Binns and Kelly-Lyth (2022), 'Directly Discriminatory Algorithms', Mod Law Rev 86(1): 144-175 (PMC10087838). It names 'proxy discrimination' as 'a common cause of algorithmic bias'. In its example, Amazon's hiring system, trained on historic data, 'quickly learned to penalise applications from graduates of two all-women's colleges' because 'some of the correlations between applicant traits and the likelihood of success were linked to sex'. It also notes 'less favourable treatment ... caused by correlations between an ADMS' features and protected characteristics'. So removing a protected attribute does not stop discrimination through correlated features. 'Where people live' is the toy's illustration of such a feature (c1-c3, verified). Checking outcomes by group is the check the claim draws from that. Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan and Pedreshi et al. 2008 are not opened.

recall.question: A hiring model is trained on past hiring decisions with the gender column removed. It still uses which sports club applicants list. Can it treat men and women differently?
options: Yes, if club membership tracks gender and the past decisions were biased
Only if someone adds the gender column back
recall.why: A feature correlated with the group carries the group into the model, so it can copy biased past decisions. Check outcomes by group, not just which columns go in.
